title: Jake Heller — From Idea to $650M Exit (Casetext / CoCounsel)
author: Jake Heller

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Heller accepts the cluster’s proposition that organisational value depends on implementation and adoption rather than software capability alone. He materially extends it from internal workflow redesign to vendor-side product strategy: durable revenue and defensibility require integrations, quality checks, thoughtful rollout, training and hands-on customer support, while pilots and superior interfaces alone may not produce sustained use.
qs: It's the human interactions with your support, customer success, with the founder, um it's training, it's, you know, everything around it.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Heller supports the cluster’s core proposition that advanced generative AI materially broadens legal software’s capabilities and can underpin a specialist legal assistant. Casetext’s sustained legal-AI research and GPT-4-driven pivot to CoCounsel align with specialist product value, though the source offers little evidence on workflow layers, lawyer–engineer collaboration, human verification or comparative performance.
qs: At KStex, we've been focused for, you know, the vast majority of our experience on a deep conviction that AI when applied to law can make a huge difference.

st.t: Startup scaling: Founder context can become bottleneck
st.an: Heller supports the cluster’s product-led organising principle: hiring, marketing, culture and other CEO responsibilities should serve product–market fit and customer value rather than become independent goals. His evidence does not address the cluster’s separate claims about founder bottlenecks, delegation or explicit decision rights.

kp.k: Early GPT-4 access prompted a wholesale product pivot
kp.d: Heller reports that Casetext received GPT-4 access in summer 2022 while generating approximately $20 million in revenue with approximately 100 employees, then stopped existing work to build CoCounsel. He describes the subsequent acquisition by Thomson Reuters for $650 million in cash. This is a founder's retrospective account, including his promotional claim that CoCounsel was the first and remains the best legal AI assistant, rather than comparative evidence.
qs: we got really early access to GPT4 like summer 2022
we were like $20 million in revenue we were doing great I had like 100 people and we stopped  everything that we were doing
we were acquired by Thompson Reuters uh not about two years ago for $650 million in cash

kp.k: Legal AI opportunities encompass assistance, substitution and unprecedented scale
kp.d: Heller distinguishes assisting professionals, replacing work through AI-powered service businesses, and undertaking work previously uneconomic for humans. He places CoCounsel in the assistance category, covering document reading, research and contract review. An AI-powered law firm is a proposed substitution model, not a description of Casetext. His third category includes parallel processing of hundreds of millions of documents that firms would not otherwise pay humans to read, categorize, summarize and index.
qs: That's what we built at co-consel. Lawyers need a lot of help reading a lot of documents, doing research, reviewing contracts, marking them up, making red lines, sending them to opposing council.
The second big category is just replacing the work altogether. People currently hire lawyers. What if we just became a law firm powered by AI?
But now that AI is here, you can have thousands of instances of Gemini 2.0, Flash, or whatever, read over every document. The previously unthinkable is now thinkable.

kp.k: Labour expenditure expands AI's proposed addressable market
kp.d: Heller argues that existing payments for human tasks reveal demand more clearly than speculative software ideas. He contrasts software-seat budgets with professionals' combined salaries, claiming AI applications could address markets 10, 100 or even a thousand times larger. These are entrepreneurial market estimates, not measured legal-market growth. Looking back, he characterizes pre-LLM legal software as a small fraction of lawyers' revenues and its benefits as incremental relative to the impact he attributes to LLMs.
qs: we already know what people want because they're paying people to do it.
today, the actual amount of money that we already know  people and companies are willing to spend is the combined salaries of all the people they're currently paying to do the job.
the amount of money that you can make with your new applications with AI has gone up by a factor of 10, 100, or even a thousand compared to what it used to be.
we were only making incremental changes to the workflow and outputs of the people we were serving

kp.k: Automation could broaden access to currently unaffordable legal help
kp.d: Heller asserts, without supplying a study in the transcript, that over 85% of low-income people lack access to legal services. He predicts that making lawyers 100 times faster and 10 times cheaper, or delivering services through AI-powered law firms, could enable acceptance of clients currently turned away for inability to pay. His broader optimistic argument treats job replacement as a route to democratizing expensive services and unlocking new activities, rather than documenting realized access-to-justice outcomes.
qs: In the field we worked in in law, over 85% of people who are low income don't get access to legal services.
if you could help make lawyers 100x faster and 10x cheaper or you know frankly just provide those services yourself as a new law firm powered by AI
where lawyers have to turn away clients because they did not have enough money  you can now say yes

kp.k: Domain expertise should determine workflow design
kp.d: Heller recommends learning what professionals actually do and designing backwards from how an excellent practitioner would perform with effectively unlimited resources. He reports that his co-founders were lawyers and 30 to 40% of the company, including coders, were lawyers. He also recommends acquiring expertise through field observation, practitioner conversations or an expert co-founder rather than assuming how work is performed.
qs: It was helpful for us that that I was a lawyer, my co-founders were lawyers, 30 to 40% of my company, even the coders were lawyers because we actually lived it.

How would the best person in that field do this if they had like unlimited time and unlimited resources like a thousand AIs that can all work in, you know, simultaneously to accomplish this task, right?
find out what what are the specific things that people do that you can assist or replace.

kp.k: Research automation decomposes expert work into explicit steps
kp.d: Heller describes building a version of deep research two and a half years earlier by decomposing legal research into clarification, planning, dozens of searches, careful reading of hundreds of results, relevance filtering, note-taking, synthesis and accuracy checks. He explains that individual stages become prompts or code, including citation comparison against original sources. These are described product-design mechanisms, not evidence that legal research can safely dispense with human checking.
qs: we did a version of deep research two and a half years ago.
They they might execute dozens of searches might that might bring back hundreds of different results.
One prompt might be like, here's a here's a footnote in the essay, here's the original resource. Is this thing, you know, accurately cited or not?

kp.k: Prefer simple workflows where expert procedures are stable
kp.d: Heller says much of CoCounsel followed fixed sequences of six or seven steps implemented in Python. He recommends conventional software rather than prompts for deterministic operations or calculations because prompts are slow and expensive. He reserves more agentic designs for tasks requiring context-dependent plans, resources or searches, while warning that their quality is harder to ensure.
qs: if it's like deterministic or it's like a math  calculation or something like that, that's better. prompts are slow and expensive.
Every  time you do this task, you're basically going to take the same six or seven steps.
That's how you get to something that's a little bit more  agentic. That's harder to make sure it's good.

kp.k: Evaluation separates reliable products from impressive demonstrations
kp.d: Heller argues that demo-level systems with 60 to 70% accuracy may attract investment and pilots yet fail in practice. He recommends domain-expert definitions of good performance for both the whole task and each microtask, objectively gradable outputs where possible, and held-out examples to avoid tailoring prompts only to known tests. This is development evaluation, not a reported independent benchmark or a measured rate of legal hallucinations.
qs: they build like demo level stuff that frankly is like 60 to 70% accurate.
This is true of the overall task like complete this research for me, but also each microtask necessary to complete the overall task
have a hold out set and don't, you know, look at those while you're while you're writing your prompts. Make sure it also works on those.

kp.k: Prompt improvement requires sustained testing and customer feedback
kp.d: Heller claims intensive prompting and expanding evaluations over roughly two weeks can move performance from around 60% to 97%, with remaining cases sometimes resembling human judgment calls. As a rough beta-readiness guide, he recommends 100 tests per prompt and 100 for the overall task, passing 99 out of 100, and preferably a thousand tests. These are heuristics rather than validated general thresholds. He recommends explaining beta limitations, turning customer failures into tests, comparing new models and continually updating prompts; he reports that real customer incidents eventually supplied more evaluations than laboratory examples.
qs: you're going to get to something that passes like 97% of the time. And the 3% is kind of explainable. It's like a human would it's like a judgment call almost.
What I recommend is like pre-production,  maybe in like beta, get to a 100, you know, tests per prompt and 100 tests for the overall task.
If you're passing like 99 out of 100, again, you should feel pretty good about where you are, right?
We've added much more eval at this point from real things that happened to real customers than the ones we came up with in the lab.

kp.k: AI service pricing can capture value beyond software subscriptions
kp.d: Heller highlights businesses delivering completed contract reviews, possibly with a human in the loop, rather than merely selling tools. His example contrasts $1,000 per review at a traditional firm with $500 from an AI-enabled provider and $20 monthly software subscriptions. He recommends pricing by customer value, including for previously infeasible work, while forecasting competitive price reductions that could ultimately make lawyer-like services available for 10 cents or one cent on the dollar. The examples and forecasts are not presented as a systematic pricing study.
qs: They're like doing the full service. Maybe there's a human in the loop.
this would usually cost somebody $1,000 per contract to review if they went with a traditional law firm. They're charging $500 per contract.
Price it according to the value you're  selling it.
you will end up charging a lot less than the people were which I think is probably a good thing at the end of the day for society

kp.k: Customer budget preferences can preserve per-seat pricing
kp.d: Heller reports that Casetext considered usage pricing but customers preferred consistent annual spending even if it cost more. He says they wanted $6,000 per seat, equivalent to $500 monthly. His recommendation is to accommodate purchasing preferences rather than assume that AI-enabled services must be priced per task; the preference is a customer view reported by the vendor.
qs: when we asked our customers, they said, "Listen, I'd rather pay more, but make it like consistent throughout the year, then potentially pay less and pay per use."
our customers wanted to pay $6,000  per seat.
our customers wanted wanted predictable budgeting. Give it to them, right?

kp.k: Trust requires comparison with established human providers
kp.d: Heller argues that organizations face pressure to try AI but remain uncertain about unfamiliar systems, whereas they know how to train, coach or fire people. He recommends side-by-side comparisons with existing law firms or accountants, studies and pilots to establish relative speed, quality and differences in results. This is a recommended adoption strategy, not a reported finding that AI outperforms those providers.
qs: there's also this trust gap because they used to do this thing by asking people and they can fire people, they can train people, they can coach people
Keep your law firm and then use our thing side by side  and then compare. How fast are we? How good were we? How different were the results?
do studies do pilots there are so many ways that you can do this

kp.k: Paid pilots do not establish durable recurring revenue
kp.d: Drawing on his post-exit angel investing experience, Heller says some startups reporting $10 million ARR are counting substantial six-month pilot payments that may not convert. He predicts a 'mass extinction event' as pilot revenue fails to become continuing business. He therefore emphasizes deliberate onboarding, training, customer success and hands-on implementation, including deployed engineers, as part of the product rather than optional additions.
qs: there are a lot of companies like our ARR is $10 million and you dig under the surface and it's like oh yeah we have a pilot for like six months and they pay us a lot of money for that pilot.
a lot of those pilots are not converting to real revenue and there's going to be a mass extinction event
your product isn't just the pixels on the screen.
It's the human interactions with your support, customer success, with the founder, um it's training

kp.k: Product quality and implementation create commercial differentiation
kp.d: Heller attributes improved demand after CoCounsel's launch to product quality, word-of-mouth referrals and unsolicited news coverage, contrasting this with weaker results from experienced sales and marketing leaders selling the earlier product. He recommends maintaining product-market fit as the organizing objective at every funding stage. In response to the concern that nonproprietary models yield mere 'GPT wrappers,' he argues that integrations, checks, model selection and painstaking prompt development accumulated over years create defensibility.
qs: When we had an awesome product, all of a sudden people were referring us by word of mouth.
those sales people became like order takers.
How many little pieces you have to build, how many data integrations, how many checks, how fine-tuned the prompts need to be, how you have to pick your models super well.
you spend like two years just doing nothing but that.

kp.k: Already-outsourced tasks offer promising automation entry points
kp.d: Heller recommends selecting large, widely shared problems where domain knowledge is available, particularly roles customers already outsource abroad. He reasons that willingness to outsource signals openness to AI substitution, whereas identity-defining work may encounter resistance, illustrated by Pixar storytelling. He advises founders not to be deterred by competitors because he expects many service markets to be large enough for multiple winners; this is strategic judgment rather than market-concentration evidence.
qs: what are the kinds of roles that people are currently outsourcing say to another country, right? If it's something that they're willing to do that for, then that's probably a pretty good target for what AI could take over.
Try to try to find the parts that are already outsourced.
There's not going to be a single company that's going to win this entire market for for the vast majority of them.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Heller distinguishes three AI opportunities: assisting professionals, replacing service delivery, and undertaking work previously impractical at human labour costs.
pts.d: Heller describes CoCounsel as an assistant for lawyers doing document reading, research, contract review and redlining. Separately, he proposes AI-powered law firms that deliver services rather than merely selling software. His third category is large-scale document analysis: using many model instances to read, categorise, summarise and index hundreds of millions of documents. These are distinct augmentation, substitution and expanded-capability claims; he does not say CoCounsel itself became a law firm.

pts.k: Heller claims LLMs substantially increased the practical impact of Casetext's products compared with its earlier legal software.
pts.d: Drawing on his founder experience, Heller contrasts incremental pre-LLM workflow improvements with helping more lawyers become substantially more effective and efficient and replacing some of their work. He reports that Casetext stopped its existing development programme after receiving early GPT-4 access in summer 2022, despite already having about $20 million in revenue and approximately 100 employees. He presents the resulting CoCounsel product and $650 million cash acquisition as a commercial success story, and calls CoCounsel the first and, in his opinion, still the best legal AI assistant. The transcript provides no comparative productivity study or independent product ranking.

pts.k: AI can expand providers' addressable markets from software budgets toward spending on professional labour and services.
pts.d: Heller argues that traditional seat-based legal software captured only a small fraction of lawyers' economic activity. AI applications that perform paid work can instead target the salaries or service fees already paid to people, including paralegals and other professionals. He describes potential market or revenue-opportunity increases of 10, 100 or 1,000 times. These are illustrative entrepreneurial claims, not a documented estimate that all professional salary spending will transfer to AI vendors.

pts.k: Heller predicts that cheaper AI-assisted or AI-delivered legal services could broaden access for people currently unable to afford lawyers.
pts.d: Heller states that over 85% of low-income people lack access to legal services, without identifying a source or defining the statistic. He conditionally argues that making lawyers 100 times faster and 10 times cheaper, or delivering services through an AI-powered law firm, would let providers accept clients previously turned away for lack of money. The speed and cost figures are hypothetical conditions, not reported CoCounsel results. More broadly, he expects replacing or substantially assisting existing jobs to unlock new activities and democratise formerly expensive professional help.

pts.k: Heller claims reliable professional AI requires domain-informed task decomposition and sustained evaluation, rather than a convincing demonstration alone.
pts.d: He describes modelling legal research on an expert's process: clarifying the request, planning, searching, reading and filtering authorities, taking notes, writing an answer and checking citations. Steps become prompts or conventional code. Fixed processes suit deterministic workflows; circumstances requiring different plans or resources may require more agentic systems, which he says are harder to assure. He claims sustained prompting and evaluation can move illustrative pass rates from roughly 60% to 97%, with remaining errors sometimes resembling human judgment calls. He recommends around 100 tests per prompt and overall task before beta, preferably more, a holdout set, and ongoing tests derived from customer failures. These percentages are development guidance, not a disclosed legal benchmark or measured hallucination rate. Automated citation checking within the workflow is not evidence of human verification before legal reliance.

pts.k: AI enables service-based and value-based pricing, but customer budgeting preferences can preserve seat-based subscriptions.
pts.d: Heller describes unnamed companies delivering complete contract review, possibly with a human in the loop, for $500 per contract rather than a traditional law firm's $1,000. This illustrates AI-enabled service provision rather than software licensing. He recommends pricing according to value, while reporting that his own customers preferred predictable annual seat pricing of $6,000, equivalent to $500 monthly, over variable usage charges. For work previously impractical for humans, he suggests discussing the customer's value or avoided costs and potentially charging 10–20% of that value; this is advice, not a reported market standard.

pts.k: Heller predicts competition will drive AI-delivered professional service prices far below human-service prices.
pts.d: He qualifies his salary-based market opportunity argument: providers may initially charge near human prices, but successive competitors will undercut them. Unless the market is protected, he expects substantially lower prices, illustrating future legal services at 10 cents or one cent on the dollar. He presents this as beneficial for society but adverse for providers' pricing power. No date, quantified competitive model or evidence of those ultimate price levels is supplied.

pts.k: Trust, implementation and real use determine whether interest in professional AI becomes durable revenue.
pts.d: Heller argues that buyers are unfamiliar with relying on AI instead of people, despite strong organisational pressure to try it. He recommends side-by-side comparisons with incumbent law firms, studies and pilots to build trust, without reporting results from such comparisons. From his post-exit angel-investor experience, he warns that high reported annual recurring revenue may actually be temporary pilot revenue and predicts a startup 'mass extinction event' as pilots fail to convert. Training, customer success and hands-on deployment are conditions for retention. Separately, he attributes Casetext's stronger word-of-mouth demand and easier selling to its improved LLM product, and argues that integrations, checks, model selection and painstaking prompting can create defensibility even when underlying models are not proprietary.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is Heller's first-person product-building, customer and investing experience; broader market and social outcomes are projections.
pts.d: Heller grounds his account in his legal career, lawyer co-founders, a workforce he says was 30–40% lawyers, early GPT-4 development, customer pricing conversations, customer-derived evaluations and post-exit investing. He reports business figures and unnamed service-pricing examples, but supplies no underlying datasets, named independent benchmarks, controlled productivity comparisons or supporting citations for the access-to-justice statistic. His claims about market expansion, widespread affordability, future job changes and competitive price compression are arguments and predictions. Suggested evaluation pass rates should not be treated as verified production accuracy. His assertion that evaluation is widely neglected is likewise not supported by a survey in the transcript.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The source mixes retrospective product experience, present opportunities and mostly undated future predictions.
pts.d: The supplied document is labelled 2026, while Heller's account uses relative expressions such as research development 'two and a half years ago' and acquisition approximately two years earlier; those expressions should not be converted into independently established dates. Summer 2022 is explicitly given for early GPT-4 access. He treats assistance, AI-powered service delivery and very large document workloads as current opportunities. Wider access depends on substantial cost and productivity improvements; reliability depends on domain expertise, iterative testing and continued work as models and customer usage change; commercial durability depends on adoption and pilot conversion. Price erosion is conditional on competition rather than a protected market. His broad suggestion that present work will feel antiquated in '10 or 15 or 100 years' is not a specific legal-employment forecast.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Heller identifies consequences for lawyers and other workers, incumbent and AI-native providers, enterprise buyers, underserved individuals and AI startups.
pts.d: Lawyers receive assistance and may have parts of their work replaced; paralegals are among the paid roles he identifies as automation opportunities. Traditional law firms face possible competition from AI-powered service providers, while firms with enormous document collections gain capabilities previously too expensive to use. Corporate clients may buy lower-cost contract review and favour predictable budgets, but need evidence and support to trust new systems. Low-income individuals could gain access to legal help, a separate benefit from enterprise savings. Legal-AI vendors and AI-native service businesses may pursue larger revenue opportunities but face implementation costs, failed pilots and price competition. Beyond law, Heller extends similar claims to customer support, insurance, accounting, finance, personal assistance and physical services. He does not quantify legal job losses or predict a particular law-firm staffing structure.
